CSA Z662 integrity management basics for pipeline operators

Direct answer: CSA Z662 is Canada's standard for oil and gas pipeline systems. It covers design, construction, operation, maintenance, deactivation and abandonment. Canadian regulators require operators to run an integrity management program (IMP) built on it. Federally, the Canada Energy Regulator's Onshore Pipeline Regulations require one. British Columbia requires an IMP that complies with Z662 and its Annex N. Alberta requires integrity management manuals with Z662 as the minimum technical requirement.

The section above covers Z662 from the NDE contractor's side, mainly the Clause 7 construction-inspection rules. This section is for the operator: what an IMP has to do, which regulator requires it, how integrity is assessed, where field NDE fits, and how Z662 compares with US integrity management rules under 49 CFR 192 and 195. Z662 is copyrighted. Nothing here reproduces its text, and annex and clause references are given only where a public regulation cites them. The current edition is CSA Z662:23. Buy it from CSA Group for the wording.

Which regulator requires an integrity management program

Direct answer: Federally regulated pipelines, meaning interprovincial and international lines, answer to the Canada Energy Regulator. Most other pipelines answer to the provincial energy regulator in the province where they run. All of them use Z662 as the technical basis, but each regulation words the IMP duty differently, so read the one that actually applies to your line.

Regulator and instrumentWhat it requires (paraphrased)How Z662 is brought in
Canada Energy Regulator: Onshore Pipeline Regulations (SOR/99-294)Section 40: develop, implement and maintain an IMP that anticipates, prevents, manages and mitigates conditions that could harm safety or the environment, across design, construction, operation, maintenance and abandonment. Section 41: document any defect beyond what Z662 allows, its likely cause and the corrective actionSection 4 requires compliance with CSA Z662, along with Z276, Z341 and Z246.1 where they apply, "as amended from time to time". If the regulations and a standard conflict, the regulations prevail
British Columbia: Pipeline Regulation (B.C. Reg. 281/2010), administered by the BC Energy RegulatorSection 7: a permit holder must not operate a pipeline until it has prepared an IMP that complies with CSA Z662 and Annex NSection 3: design, construction, operation, maintenance, deactivation, reactivation and abandonment must follow Z662 and its Annex A
Alberta: Pipeline Rules (Alta. Reg. 91/2005), administered by the Alberta Energy RegulatorSection 7: keep manuals with procedures for operation, corrosion control, integrity management, maintenance and repair. Include provisions to evaluate and mitigate stress corrosion cracking where coatings are disbonded or not working. Be able to show the procedures are being followedSection 9: references are to the latest CSA edition, and Z662 sets the minimum requirements for design, construction, testing, operation, maintenance, repair and leak detection. Annex E leak detection is mandatory for liquid hydrocarbon pipelines
Ontario: TSSA Fuels Safety programPipelines under TSSA's jurisdiction are handled by the Fuels Safety program, not the boiler and pressure vessel programTSSA's BPV Code Adoption Document points to the Fuels Safety adoption document for the Z662 edition

The quotations above come from the consolidated regulations we reviewed. The Alberta consolidation we read was current to 2020, and Alberta has issued AER directives since then, including a July 2026 edition of Directive 077 that cites specific Z662 clauses. Confirm the current text with the regulator before you build an audit checklist on it. Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Quebec and the Atlantic provinces each have their own pipeline regulators and instruments. Check each one rather than assuming the Alberta or BC wording applies.

What Annex N asks an integrity management program to do

Direct answer: Annex N of Z662 gives guidelines for a pipeline system integrity management program. It is written as a guideline, but BC's Pipeline Regulation makes compliance with it a condition of operating. In plain terms, an IMP built to Annex N keeps records, identifies hazards, assesses risk and condition, mitigates, and keeps improving, all within a management system.

Without reproducing the annex, the elements regulators and auditors expect to see in a Z662 IMP are these:

  • Policy, accountability and a management system. Who owns integrity decisions, with resources, competence and document control. Z662 ties the IMP to the operator's safety and loss management system (Annex A, which BC's regulation also names).
  • Records and data integration. Pipe and coating specifications, construction and pressure-test records, operating pressure and product history, cathodic protection data, in-line inspection results, dig reports, leaks, failures and third-party damage, brought together so that one threat is not assessed without the others.
  • Hazard identification. External and internal corrosion, stress corrosion cracking, manufacturing and construction defects, mechanical damage, ground movement and geotechnical hazards, incorrect operation, and equipment failure at facilities.
  • Risk and condition assessment. Ranking segments by likelihood and consequence, then choosing an assessment method for each threat: in-line inspection, pressure testing, or direct assessment by excavation.
  • Mitigation and repair. Responses to assessment results, including pressure reduction, repair, recoating, cathodic protection improvement, monitoring and geohazard work, with a documented engineering basis.
  • Continual improvement. Performance measures, audits, incident investigation and management review that feed back into the plan.

Two practical points come out of the regulations. First, CER section 41 makes defect documentation a legal record. Each defect beyond Z662 limits needs its particulars, likely cause and corrective action written down. Second, Alberta's SCC provision means operators of lines with disbonded coating need a written SCC evaluation, not just a corrosion programme.

How integrity is assessed, and where field NDE fits

Direct answer: Integrity is assessed in three main ways: in-line inspection (ILI) by instrumented tools travelling through the pipe, hydrostatic pressure testing, and direct assessment by excavation. Field NDE is central to the third. It verifies ILI calls at integrity digs, sizes wall loss and cracks, characterises SCC colonies, and inspects piping that tools cannot reach.

ILI tools, often called pigs, use magnetic flux leakage, ultrasonic or EMAT technologies to report metal loss, cracks, dents and geometry along the line. They are run by specialist ILI vendors. Atlantis does not run ILI tools. What an ILI report produces is a list of anomalies with predicted dimensions and a dig programme. At each dig, the predicted size has to be measured in the ditch, because repair decisions and tool-performance validation depend on those measured dimensions.

ThreatTypical system-level assessmentField NDE at the dig or facilityWhat the NDE cannot decide
External corrosionMFL or UT in-line inspection, CP surveysUT thickness grids or phased array corrosion mapping to measure remaining wall and profile, plus pit depth measurementWhether the feature is acceptable. That is the operator's engineering assessment against Z662
Internal corrosionILI, internal corrosion modelling, coupon and probe monitoringExternal UT and corrosion mapping at low points, drips and dead legs, and radiography where profile mattersCorrosion rate trends without repeat measurements at the same locations
Stress corrosion crackingCrack-detection ILI, SCC susceptibility modelling, hydrotestCoating removal followed by MT (often wet fluorescent) to find and map SCC colonies, and UT or phased array for crack depth where the procedure allowsCrack growth rate and the safe pressure. Those are engineering calculations
Mechanical damage and dentsGeometry and caliper ILIDimensional measurement of the dent, plus MT at the dent for gouges or cracksStrain-based acceptance, which belongs to the engineer
Facility piping and crossingsOften not piggableGuided wave screening with UT follow-up, and CUI screening on insulated station pipingGuided wave is a screening tool, so its calls need confirmation by direct measurement

Integrity-dig NDE is only useful if it can be tied back to the ILI report. That means recording girth weld references, odometer and reference-point distances, clock position, and the coating condition found. Repair and acceptance decisions are made by the operator's integrity engineers using Z662's defect assessment rules and their own procedures. That is an engineering assessment, not an NDE deliverable. See guided wave testing, corrosion mapping, MT for pipelines and UT for pipelines.

CSA Z662 versus US integrity management rules

Direct answer: US federal rules apply prescriptive integrity management requirements tied to high consequence areas: 49 CFR 192 Subpart O for gas transmission and 49 CFR 195.452 for hazardous liquid lines. Canadian regulators require a system-wide IMP based on Z662 and a management system. Cross-border operators usually run one programme mapped to both sets of rules.

TopicCanada (Z662 and regulator)United States (PHMSA)
Scope of the IMP dutyThe whole pipeline system, under the regulator's IMP requirement and Z662Gas transmission IM focuses on high consequence areas. Liquid IM covers segments that could affect high consequence areas. Further rules have extended assessment beyond HCAs in some cases
Technical basisCSA Z662, including its annexes as the regulator calls them inThe regulations themselves, with ASME B31.8S incorporated for gas IM and API standards for liquids
Assessment intervalsSet by the operator's IMP and engineering basis, subject to regulator reviewMaximum reassessment intervals are written into the regulations
Defect recordsCER: document defects beyond Z662 limits, their cause and the corrective actionSpecific repair-criteria timelines for discovered conditions

For the US side in more depth, see pipeline integrity management under 49 CFR 192 and 195, ASME B31.8 and ASME B31.4.

NDE personnel on Z662 work

Direct answer: Z662's construction-inspection clauses tie radiographers and ultrasonic inspectors to CAN/CGSB-48.9712 qualification. Integrity-dig NDE is governed by the operator's own specification, which often asks for the same scheme. Since CGSB closed on 1 April 2026, that certification has continued through Natural Resources Canada's NDT Certification Body.

Before mobilising any NDE crew to a Canadian pipeline, confirm in writing which certification scheme the operator's specification requires for each method. Atlantis technicians are certified to ASNT SNT-TC-1A under ASNT NDT Level III oversight. If a Z662 clause or the operator's specification requires CAN/CGSB-48.9712 certification, that requirement governs, and we will tell you at scoping what we can staff. Industrial radiography anywhere in Canada also requires Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission licensing for the exposure device and certified exposure device operators. See NRCan NDT certification and CNSC requirements.

Common mistakes in Z662 integrity programmes

  • An IMP that only exists on paper. Alberta's rules require operators to be able to show the procedures are being followed, and CER and BC audits test the same thing.
  • Threats assessed in isolation. A corrosion feature found at a dent, or an SCC colony found where coating has failed, needs both threats assessed together. Data integration exists to catch exactly that.
  • Dig data that cannot be matched to ILI. Without girth weld references and distances, measured features cannot validate tool performance, and the next ILI run cannot be compared with this one.
  • Undocumented defects. Under CER section 41, a defect beyond Z662 limits needs a written record of its particulars, likely cause and corrective action, even when it is repaired the same day.
  • Edition drift. Several regulators reference the latest Z662 edition, so a new edition can apply without a separate adoption date. Procedures written to an older edition become non-compliant without anyone noticing.
  • Using the wrong certification wording. Specifications that still say "CGSB certified" should be updated to name NRCan's NDTCB and CAN/CGSB-48.9712.

How Atlantis supports Z662 integrity programmes

Atlantis NDT performs field NDE for operators' integrity programmes: UT thickness and phased array corrosion mapping at integrity digs, MT for SCC colony mapping, guided wave screening with UT follow-up on station piping and crossings, and CUI screening. The work is done by ASNT-certified technicians under ASNT NDT Level III oversight, where the operator's specification accepts that scheme. We report measured dimensions tied to your ILI references. Your integrity engineers own the IMP, the defect assessment and the repair decision. We do not run in-line inspection tools and we do not perform fitness-for-service or engineering critical assessments. See pipeline inspection services and NDT consulting in Canada. We have completed 1,500+ inspection activities. Send your dig programme for a quote within 24 hours.

CSA Z662 integrity management: frequently asked questions

What is a CSA Z662 integrity management program?

It is the operator's documented programme for anticipating, preventing, managing and mitigating conditions that could harm pipeline safety or the environment, built on Z662 and the regulator's IMP requirement. Annex N of Z662 gives the guidelines.

Is CSA Z662 Annex N mandatory?

Annex N is written as a guideline, but BC's Pipeline Regulation requires an IMP that complies with Z662 and Annex N before a pipeline operates. Other regulators word it differently, so check your jurisdiction.

What does the CER Onshore Pipeline Regulations require for integrity management?

Section 40 requires an IMP covering design, construction, operation, maintenance and abandonment. Section 41 requires documentation of any defect beyond Z662 limits, its likely cause and the corrective action.

What is the current edition of CSA Z662?

CSA Z662:23. Because some regulators reference the latest edition, confirm the date it applies to your pipeline with your regulator.

How does CSA Z662 compare with ASME B31.8 and 49 CFR 192?

Z662 combines design, construction, operation and integrity management in one Canadian standard. In the US, ASME B31.8 covers gas pipeline design and construction, B31.8S and 49 CFR 192 Subpart O cover gas integrity management, and 49 CFR 195 covers liquids.

Does Atlantis run in-line inspection pigs?

No. ILI is run by specialist tool vendors. Atlantis performs field NDE at integrity digs and on facility piping to verify and size what ILI reports.

Who decides whether a pipeline defect is acceptable under Z662?

The operator's integrity engineers, using Z662's assessment rules and their own procedures, subject to regulator oversight. NDE supplies the measurements. Ask us to scope NDE for your next dig season.

What NDE finds stress corrosion cracking on pipelines?

After coating removal, MT (often wet fluorescent) finds and maps SCC colonies, and UT or phased array can estimate crack depth where the procedure allows. Crack-detection ILI and hydrotesting assess SCC at system level.
